parts.proper_answer: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Kinetic Energy Means**
Think of kinetic energy as stored motion. Any mass $m$ moving with speed $v$ has the ability to do work as it slows down, and that ability is its kinetic energy.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: A cannon fires a shell vertically upwards. The shell leaves the cannon with a speed of $80\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and a kinetic energy of $480\text{ J}$. The shell then rises to a maximum height of $210\text{ m}$. The effect of air resistance is significant.
parts.text: Show that the mass of the shell is $0.15\text{ kg}$.
hints: Hint 1: You are given the starting kinetic energy and the starting speed. Think about which quantities kinetic energy depends on and which one is unknown here.
Hint 2: Write $E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ and rearrange for $m$ before substituting $E_k = 480\text{ J}$ and $v = 80\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start From The Governing Law**
A moving mass has kinetic energy linked to its mass and speed by $$E_k = \frac{1}{2}mv^2$$ Here you know $E_k$ and $v$, and $m$ is the unknown.

Step 2: **Rearrange Then Substitute**
Rearrange for mass first: $$m = \frac{2E_k}{v^2}$$ Then put the numbers in: $$m = \frac{2 \times 480}{80^2} = \frac{960}{6400} = 0.15\text{ kg}$$ This is the required show-that result.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Determine the average force due to the air resistance acting on the shell as it moves from the cannon to its maximum height.
hints: Hint 1: The 170 J of energy lost to the air is removed over the whole 210 m rise. Think about how work links a force to the distance it acts over.
Hint 2: Use average work $W = Fs$ along the line of motion, so $F = W/s = 170/210$ and give the answer in $\text{N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Work To Average Force**
Work done by a constant or average force in the direction of motion is $$W = Fs$$ Here $W = 170\text{ J}$ is spread over distance $s = 210\text{ m}$ upward.

Step 2: **Calculate The Average Resistive Force**
Rearrange and substitute: $$F = \frac{W}{s} = \frac{170}{210} \approx 0.81\text{ N}$$ This is the average air resistance opposing the upward motion.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text:
The shell leaves the cannon at time $t = 0$ and reaches maximum height at time $t = T$.

On Fig. 2.1, sketch the variation with time $t$ of the velocity $v$ of the shell from time $t = 0$ to time $t = T$. Numerical values of $v$ and $t$ are not required.
{{figure:figure_2_1}}
Fig. 2.1

markscheme_points.text: curved line from positive value on v-axis to $(T, 0)$

hints: Hint 1: At $t = 0$ the velocity is at its maximum positive value and at $t = T$ it must be zero at the top. Think about whether the slowing down is uniform when air resistance is significant.

Hint 2: Recall gradient of a $v$-$t$ graph is acceleration. As speed falls, air resistance falls, so total downward force and deceleration get smaller - sketch a curve whose downward slope gets less steep.
parts.proper_answer: Curved line starting at positive $v$ on the $v$-axis and ending at $(T,0)$ with magnitude of gradient decreasing with time.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Start And End Points**
Upward is positive. At $t = 0$, $v$ is maximum at $80\text{ m s}^{-1}$. At $t = T$ at maximum height, $v = 0$. So your line goes from the positive $v$-axis down to $(T,0)$.

Step 2: **Why The Graph Curves**
Gradient of $v$ against $t$ is acceleration. The shell slows down due to weight plus air resistance downward. As $v$ drops, air resistance drops, so resultant downward force drops and deceleration drops. That means the $v$-$t$ graph is steep at first and then flattens, so the magnitude of the negative gradient decreases. Draw a smooth curve, concave upwards, not a straight line.

parts.label: (b)(v)
parts.text:
The force due to the air resistance is a vector quantity.

Compare the force due to the air resistance acting on the shell as it rises with the force due to the air resistance as it falls.

markscheme_points.text: as shell rises force decreases and as shell falls force increases
as shell rises force is downward and as shell falls force is upward
as shell rises the force decreases and is downward
as shell falls the force increases and is upward

hints: Hint 1: Air resistance is a vector that always opposes the velocity. Think about the direction of motion on the way up compared to the way down.
Hint 2: The size of air resistance grows with speed. Think about how speed changes during the rise and during the fall, and what that means for the size of the force in each stage.
parts.proper_answer: On the way up the air resistance acts downwards and its magnitude decreases as speed decreases. On the way down the air resistance acts upwards and its magnitude increases as speed increases.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Direction Is Always Opposite Motion**
Air resistance opposes velocity. While rising, velocity is up so resistance is down. While falling, velocity is down so resistance is up. The vector reverses direction.

Step 2: **Magnitude Follows Speed**
Air resistance is larger at larger speed. On the way up the shell slows down, so the downward resistive force gets smaller. On the way down the shell speeds up from rest, so the upward resistive force gets larger. So both magnitude and direction are different between rise and fall.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
key_concepts: conservation of energy with work done
hints: Hint 1: For the rise to 210 m, think about where the initial 480 J of kinetic energy goes - some becomes stored height energy and some is lost to the air.
Hint 2: First calculate the stored height energy from mass, $g$ and height, then find the missing energy by subtraction from the starting kinetic energy.
Hint 3: Use $\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$ with $m = 0.15\text{ kg}$, $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$, $h = 210\text{ m}$, then use work done $= 480 - \Delta E_p$.
parts.proper_answer: 1. $\Delta E_p = mgh = 0.15 \times 9.81 \times 210 = 310\text{ J}$. 2. Work done against air resistance $= 480 - 310 = 170\text{ J}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Gain In Gravitational Potential Energy**
Lifting a mass $m$ through height $h$ stores energy: $$\Delta E_p = mg\Delta h$$ With $m = 0.15\text{ kg}$, $g = 9.81\text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $\Delta h = 210\text{ m}$: $$\Delta E_p = 0.15 \times 9.81 \times 210 \approx 3.1 \times 10^2\text{ J}$$ So about $310\text{ J}$ is stored.

Step 2: **Work Done Against Air Resistance**
You started with $480\text{ J}$ of kinetic energy but only $310\text{ J}$ ends up as potential energy. The rest is removed by air resistance. By conservation of energy: $$\text{work done} = \text{initial } E_k - \text{gain in } E_p$$ $$\text{work done} = 480 - 310 = 170\text{ J}$$
